title: Al, the Underworld Dweller
summary: A demonic being who lives in the depths of the earth, luring the living underground with promises of treasure, because in Georgia the earth itself hungers.
full_text:
Al is the lord of the underworld. He lives beneath the mountains of Georgia, in caverns so deep no lamp can light them. He is massive. His body is black. His eyes are red. His voice is the sound of rock splitting.

Al does not come to the surface often. When he does, he comes for a reason. He comes for people.

Al calls to miners. He calls to men who dig into the earth for gold and silver. He whispers to them. He tells them where the richest veins are. He tells them where the deepest gold lies.

The miners follow the voice. They dig deeper. They dig past the safe layers. They dig into the dark. The earth closes behind them. The tunnel collapses. The miners do not return.

Al takes the miners underground. He keeps them as servants. They mine for him. They dig his caverns. They carry his treasure. They never see the sun again.

Al also takes women. He appears to them at night. He appears as a handsome man. He seduces them. He takes them underground. They become his brides. They live in the dark. They forget the light.

The only protection against Al is iron. An iron knife placed under the pillow keeps Al away. An iron nail driven into the doorframe keeps Al out. Iron burns Al. Iron is the one thing the underworld cannot contain.

The miners of Chiatura carry iron. They tie iron nails to their belts. They hang iron above the mine entrance. They pray to God before they descend. They do not pray to Al. To pray to Al is to belong to Al.

Al waits. He is patient. The earth is deep. The gold is deep. The miners will come.
moral: The deeper you dig, the closer you get to what waits below.
source: Georgian oral tradition, documented by Ekvtime Takaishvili

title: Amirani, the Chained Hero
summary: A Titan-like hero who defied the gods and was chained to a mountain for eternity, his chains binding him until the day a greater hero comes to free him.
full_text:
Amirani was a hero. He was stronger than any man. He was braver than any warrior. He challenged the gods. He fought them. He won.

The gods were angry. They could not kill Amirani. He was too strong. So they chained him. They chained him to the highest peak of the Caucasus. They bound his hands. They bound his feet. They bound his neck.

The chains are made of the same metal as the stars. They cannot be broken. They cannot be rusted. They cannot be cut.

Amirani hangs on the mountain. His body is exposed. The sun burns him by day. The frost freezes him by night. The eagles tear at his flesh. The flesh grows back. The eagles return. The cycle continues.

Amirani does not die. He does not scream. He waits. He waits for the hero who will come to free him. The prophecy says the hero will be born in Georgia. The hero will be stronger than Amirani. The hero will break the chains.

When the chains break, the world will change. The gods will fall. The mountains will move. The sea will dry up. A new age will begin.

The people of Georgia tell the story of Amirani to their children. They point to the mountains. They say, "There. That is where Amirani hangs. Look at the snow on the peak. That is the frost that freezes him."

The children look. They see the mountain. They see the snow. They wonder about the hero who waits.

Amirani does not wonder. He knows. The hero is coming. The chains will break. The world will change.
moral: Some heroes are measured not by their victories, but by their endurance.
source: Georgian national mythology, Mesrop Mashtots manuscripts

title: Ali, the Mountain Demon
summary: A monstrous demon who dwells in the high mountains, stealing livestock and children, because in Georgia the peaks belong to things older than faith.
full_text:
Ali is not Al. Ali is different. Al lives underground. Ali lives in the mountains. Al tempts. Ali takes.

Ali is a demon. He is large, larger than a man. His body is covered in hair. His eyes are burning. He has horns. He has hooves. He smells of sulfur.

Ali lives in the high mountains, above the tree line, where the rocks are bare and the wind never stops. He has a den. The den is filled with the bones of animals. The bones of sheep. The bones of goats. The bones of children.

Ali steals livestock. He comes down from the mountain at night. He opens the pen. He takes the best sheep. He carries them up the mountain. The shepherd wakes in the morning. The best sheep are gone.

Ali also takes children. He appears to them when they are playing alone in the fields. He appears as a beautiful horse. He lets the child ride him. The child rides. The horse runs. The horse runs up the mountain. The child does not return.

The only protection against Ali is prayer. A prayer said before entering the mountains keeps Ali away. A cross drawn on the door of the sheep pen keeps Ali out. The name of God spoken aloud burns Ali's ears.

But prayer is not always enough. Ali is strong. Ali is old. He was there before the cross. He was there before the prayer. He was there before the mountains had names.

The shepherds of Svaneti do not go above the tree line alone. They go in groups. They carry crosses. They chant prayers. They know Ali is watching from the peaks.

Ali watches. The shepherds pray. The mountains stand between them.
moral: The mountains belong to things older than faith.

title: Kaji, the Fire Spirit
summary: A spirit of fire and lightning that inhabits the hearth, protecting the home when respected and burning it when angered, because in Georgia fire is both hearth and hell.
full_text:
Kaji is the fire spirit. He lives in the hearth. He lives in the flame. He is the warmth of the house. He is the light of the kitchen. He is the fire that cooks the food.

Kaji is not evil. He is not good. He is fire. Fire does not distinguish between the meal and the house. Fire burns what it touches.

Kaji protects the home. If the family respects Kaji, if they keep the hearth clean, if they do not speak ill in the kitchen, if they offer Kaji bread and salt, Kaji protects. Kaji keeps the cold away. Kaji keeps the evil spirits away. Kaji keeps the house warm.

But if the family disrespects Kaji, if they let the hearth go cold, if they argue in the kitchen, if they spill food on the fire, Kaji burns. Kaji burns the food. Kaji burns the house. Kaji burns the family.

Kaji is also the spirit of lightning. When lightning strikes a house, that is Kaji. Kaji is punishing the family. Kaji is angry. The family must make amends. The family must offer Kaji more bread. The family must keep the hearth burning.

The people of Tbilisi keep their hearths clean. They do not argue in the kitchen. They offer Kaji bread and salt every morning. They keep the fire burning day and night.

Kaji is content. The house is warm. The family is safe.

But there are houses where the hearth is cold. There are houses where Kaji is angry. You can tell by the smell. The smell of smoke. The smell of burning. The smell of a house that did not respect its fire.

Kaji burns. The house burns. The fire does not distinguish.
moral: Fire is both hearth and hell. Treat it accordingly.
source: Georgian domestic folklore, documented by Ilia Chavchavadze

title: Devi, the Mountain Giant
summary: A race of giants who once ruled the mountains of Georgia before humans drove them into the deep caves, where they still wait to reclaim the surface.
full_text:
The Devi are giants. They are as tall as the mountains. They are as old as the rocks. They were there before the humans. They were there before the trees. They were there before the rivers carved the valleys.

The Devi ruled the surface of Georgia. They walked the mountains. They ate the animals. They drank from the rivers. They slept in the caves.

Then the humans came. The humans were small. The humans were weak. But the humans had fire. The humans had iron. The humans had God.

The humans fought the Devi. The war lasted generations. The humans burned the Devi's caves. The humans drove the Devi underground. The humans built churches on the Devi's dens.

The Devi retreated. They went deep. They went where the fire of humans could not reach. They went where the crosses could not burn them.

But the Devi did not die. The Devi wait. They wait in the deep caves. They wait in the caverns beneath the mountains. They wait for the humans to forget. They wait for the fires to go out. They wait for the crosses to crumble.

When the humans forget, the Devi will return. They will climb from the caves. They will reclaim the mountains. They will walk the surface again.

The people of Khevi say the Devi are still in the caves. They say the earthquakes are the Devi moving. They say the storms are the Devi angry. They say the avalanches are the Devi pushing against the mountains.

The people of Khevi do not enter caves alone. They do not dig too deep. They do not forget.

The Devi wait.
moral: The earth remembers who was here first, and it is patient.

title: Dze-temi, the Night Hunter
summary: A spectral hunter who rides through the night sky, chasing the souls of the dead, because in Georgia the hunt never ends.
full_text:
Dze-temi rides at night. He rides a black horse. The horse has no eyes. The horse has no rider. Dze-temi is the rider. Dze-temi is the horse. They are one.

Dze-temi hunts souls. The souls of the dead who have not crossed over. The souls who are trapped between worlds. The souls who are afraid.

Dze-temi chases them through the sky. He rides across the mountains. He rides across the valleys. He rides across the rivers. The souls run. Dze-temi follows.

When Dze-temi catches a soul, he takes it. He takes it to the underworld. He delivers it to Al. The soul is gone. The soul is underground. The soul will never return.

Dze-temi appears on nights when the moon is dark. He appears as a shadow on the horizon. He appears as a sound like hooves on stone. He appears as a wind that smells of earth and iron.

The people of Kakheti do not walk at night when the moon is dark. They stay inside. They lock the doors. They light candles. They pray.

They know Dze-temi is riding. They know the souls are running. They know the hunt is on.

Some people have seen Dze-temi. They have seen the black horse on the ridge. They have seen the shadow against the sky. They have heard the hooves. They have felt the wind.

They do not speak of it. To speak of Dze-temi is to invite Dze-temi. To speak of the hunt is to join the hunt.

The people of Kakheti keep their silence. The souls run. Dze-temi rides. The night is long.
moral: The hunt for souls never ends, and the night belongs to the hunter.

title: Dzudzerume, the Mountain Witch
summary: A mountain witch who steals children and replaces them with changelings, because in Georgia the mountains take what they want.
full_text:
Dzudzerume lives in the mountains. She is old. She is older than the trees. She is older than the rivers. She is as old as the rocks.

Dzudzerume wants children. She cannot have children of her own. She is too old. She is too stone. So she takes them.

Dzudzerume appears at night. She appears as a beautiful woman. She appears at the window. She sings to the child. The child sleeps. The child dreams of mountains. The child dreams of snow. The child dreams of a woman with stone hands.

In the morning, the child is changed. The child is quiet. The child does not cry. The child does not laugh. The child stares. The child's eyes are different. The child's eyes are old.

The mother knows. The mother has been warned. The mother checks the child. The child is not her child. The child is a changeling. The child is a stone child. The child is what Dzudzerume left behind.

The only way to get the real child back is to find Dzudzerume. You must go to the mountains. You must find her den. You must take the child back. Dzudzerume will not give the child willingly. You must trick her. You must outsmart her.

Some mothers find their children. Some mothers do not. Some mothers search the mountains forever. Some mothers never return.

The people of Tusheti name their children early. They name them before Dzudzerume can take them. They keep the names close. They whisper the names at night. The names protect the children.

Dzudzerume listens. She waits. She knows the names too.

The mountains are patient. Dzudzerume is patient. The children are not safe.
moral: The mountains take what they want, and they leave something behind.
